title: Cross-Validation
hook: One lucky or unlucky split can flatter or sink your model. Rotate the holdout and average — that's cross-validation.
key_points: k-fold splits the data into k parts, holding out each in turn as the validation set.
Every example gets used for both training and validation, just never at the same time.
Averaging across folds gives a more stable, less luck-dependent performance estimate.
It's especially valuable when data is limited and a single holdout would be noisy.
content_html: Cross-validation gives you a sturdier estimate of how a model will perform when you don't have enough data to spare a big, reliable validation set. In k-fold cross-validation you slice the data into k parts, then train k times, each time holding out a different part to validate on, and average the results.
extra_html:
How it works

Split the data into k roughly equal folds. For each round, train on k−1 of them and evaluate on the one left out, rotating until every fold has served as the holdout exactly once. Averaging the k scores smooths out the noise you'd get from any single arbitrary split, and the spread across folds also hints at how stable your model is.

Why it matters

With a small dataset, a single train/validation split can hand you a misleadingly rosy or grim number purely by chance. Cross-validation wrings more signal out of limited data and is the standard way to compare models or tune settings fairly. The cost is compute: you're training the model k times instead of once.

related.hook: If you tune and grade on the same data, you'll fool yourself. Keep a test set you never touch until the very end.

flashcards.prompt: How does k-fold cross-validation use every example for both training and validation?
flashcards.back_html: It splits data into k folds and trains k times, each time holding out a different fold to validate on, so each fold serves once as holdout.

flashcards.prompt: Why is cross-validation especially valuable with limited data?

choices.text: A single holdout split would be noisy and luck-dependent
It eliminates the need for a training set
It guarantees the model won't overfit

flashcards.explanation_html: With small data a single split can hand you a misleadingly rosy or grim number; averaging folds gives a more stable estimate.

flashcards.prompt: What is the main cost of cross-validation?

choices.text: Compute: you train the model k times instead of once
It requires labeled data, unlike a single split
It always produces a biased estimate
